title: Brothers and Sisters
author: Smallwood, Christine
summary: Christine Smallwood's sweeping literary essay on sibling relationships across canonical literature—Kafka, Sophocles, Brontë, Bernhard—argues that siblings represent the original school for tolerating otherness we did not choose. Sibling bonds threaten the fantasy of a singular, heroic self because they are relationships we can neither desire nor eliminate, only endure. Smallwood reveals how contemporary culture has optimized away unchosen relationships, failing to recognize that unchosen-ness itself performs essential developmental work in identity formation.
points: The sibling relationship is the original school for tolerating the existence of others we did not choose and cannot exit.
Siblings threaten the fantasy of a singular, heroic self precisely because they are peers we can neither desire nor eliminate, only endure.
Modern culture has optimized away unchosen relationships, not realizing that unchosen-ness performs essential developmental work.
Siblings work together as an anthropological reality—what Smallwood exposes is a culture that has severed these formative bonds while calling it liberation.
When a culture tears out the architecture of unchosen ties and inherited meanings, it should not be surprised when people cannot figure out where the walls are.
quotes: The sibling relationship is the original school for tolerating the existence of others we did not choose.
Siblings threaten the fantasy of a singular, heroic self precisely because they are peers we can neither desire nor eliminate, only endure and, sometimes, love.
A culture obsessed with self-improvement has produced astonishingly few lives worth re-living, because the entire apparatus of modern self-construction is organized around becoming impressive.

When a culture tears out the architecture of unchosen ties, it should not be surprised when the people living inside cannot figure out where the walls are.” Archived from Harper's Magazine on May 2, 2026 by Tim.
